I don't understand why there are so many collisions -- the UUID4 implementation is -- literally -- os.urandom(16). github.com/python/cpython/blob/3.12/Lib/uuid.py#L723

@JamesS have a look at the UUID-class: os.random(16) generates 16 bytes, not characters, and is passed to the UUID constructor. When you call str() on an instance of UUID you will get the hex representation of that 128 bit int. So basically you are using the "reduced" alphabet of "abcdef0123456789" instead of all lower case letters. So, way fewer combinations and more collisions. See UUID.__str__() at github.com/python/cpython/blob/…

@Stefan I don't think that's true. Yes, you have a reduced alphabet, but the string is longer. You're still working with 16 bytes worth of data. You don't lose anything by converting to hex. If you did, you wouldn't be able to convert hex back to bytes. Every 2 hex characters represents one of 256 values, just like a byte. One thing I realized from your link is that there are a few bits of version and variant info that is "static", but you still have  21^22, or 5.3×1036 (5.3 undecillion) possibilities.

@JamesS, thanks for taking the time to answer. Exactly my point. :) To represent 1 byte (256 possible combinations) in hex notation you need two hex-digits from the "hex-alphabet". As you put it: "the string is longer". But then the code in this answer truncates the hex-representation to a string of length 8: str(uuid.uuid4())[:8]. So we are left with some number between 00000000 and FFFFFFFF in hex notation. That's only 16^8 = 4,294,967,296 possible combinations, isn't it? We could represent the same number of combinations using just 32 bit (2^32 = 4,294,967,296).

@zahory: tempfile.mktemp can still generate guaranteed-unique temporary filenames without creating the files. Sure, it isn't as secure as mkstemp, but the same is true for a random generator, and of the two, mktemp is absolutely safe instead of just "pretty safe, hopefully safe enough" from non-malicious collisions. It's also simpler and probably more efficient. So I'd still look into whether you can use it, or something similar. I'd also consider the counter before going to random as a last-ditch fallback.

@zahory: You don't need the brackets you added to my answer unless you're using Python 2.3 or earlier. (random.choice(my_charset) for ch in range(8)) is a generator expression, which is a perfectly valid sequence to pass to join. But your application needs to authenticate itself without leaving a key in the source code. A way to do this is to use a counter key based on the last interaction. Kind of like car locks that change the code each time. If someone can compromise the run state of your main server then they can still get the oauth keys, but not if they only have the source code. The secrets are stored in memory. You can encrypt this counter with your ouath

with your ouath server's public key, and send it securely to your ouath server to verify. Your main application then updates it's counter key for the next interaction. One way to do this update is to have the ouath server return an open-channel nonce, and encrypt your current counter key with that nonce. The counter key remains secure as long as the RAM on your main server is secure. (of course you need to initially sync a secret with the ouath server on load but this can be done DH Key Xchange with a random session key). Finally you get another
dimension of security from the fact that your oauth server only accepts requests from your main servers domain.

That wiki is out of date and incomplete. For transaction signatures, ASN.1 DER encoding for secp256k1 is usually 72, 71, or 70 octets, and rarely less, and bitcoin adds one octet for 'sighash'. The main thing about CTR mode you have to understand is that the same counter value must not ever be used when you use the same key. The AES block size is 128 bits long which means that the counter in CTR mode must have the same size. There are different ways to think about what the counter is. Usually, we're talking about a fixed part of bits x and the variable part of bits 128 - x. The fixed part is usually set to 96 random bits when starting to encrypt a message, because it is sufficiently improbable to get the same prefix for multiple encryptions....

When the prefix is set, then the remaining bits (128-96=32) can be used to increase the counter for each block that is encrypted. For AES, that means that 68 GB or data can be encrypted before you need a new prefix (2^32 * 128 bit). If you need to encrypt more data in a single pass, you can use a 88 bit prefix and a 40 bit counter. You can't decrease the prefix length arbitrarily. You have to think about how many messages you want to encrypt. For example, if you want to encrypt more than 4 billion messages, then a prefix of 64 bit will not be enough due to the birthday problem.

Usually the data is not directly signed by the public key of the root CA certificate. The root cert is used to sign zero or more intermediate CA certificates, and CA certificate signs a leaf certificate, which signs the data, in this case a JWT. If you get the root certificate you've got the trust anchor. Now when you get the signed data which includes the leaf cert then you need to create a trust path towards the trust anchor, validate & verify all the certs, and then check the signature using the public key of the leaf certificate.

You will find an x5c parameter with a certificate chain in the JWT header. For the verification of the JWT the first certificate has to be used! In general, cryptographically secure PRNG's are rather secure, and if they have a big enough state, the chances of them going into a cycle are very slim. /dev/urandom moreover is periodically seeded by /dev/random. This seed is then mixed into the state. /dev/random is normally fed by OS entropy pools, e.g. small time differences in network cards or - if you are lucky - with a random generator within the CPU. Hence the number of random bytes is rather limited, and you may get into a state where more random bytes are required than available; in that case the application will block.

It depends on the algorithm used for generating the random number. And that in turn depends on the implementation. The security part is not so much an issue though; both are reasonably secure in most implementations; the blocking part on the other hand is worse. But it is even better to use a PRNG within your application seeded from the OS using enough entropy. In that case you can generate oodles of RNG data without having to go through the kernel at all; it may of course be a good idea to reseed using the OS after generating 1MiB to 1GiB of data.

The IV does not have to be kept secret. It is often prepended to the cyphertext, so it is known to any attacker. Another way to think about the IV is that any encrypted block (when there are many) is the IV of the next block in CBC. It is safe to transfer as is. Your approach loses sight of the overarching problem. With a simple static substitution cipher, if x corresponds to y in one word, it will correspond to y in all words. The typical approach is to calculate frequency statistics for English (or whichever language you are targeting) and assume that the ciphertext has roughly the same characteristics. Frequency statistics for English would predict that e is the most frequent character, t is second in rank, a is third, followed by o, i, n, etc.

You might want to do frequency analysis on adjacent characters or entire tokens too (here your current code could actually come in useful) but the key you seek to find is one which unlocks all the words in the text at the same time. (In real-world English you should expect some tokens to not correspond to known dictionary words.)

For example, if abc is the most frequent token in your ciphertext, a good first hypothesis is that it corresponds to "the"; but if that doesn't give useful results for other tokens in the text, fall back to increasingly less likely hypoteses, from "for" and "let" through "fat" and "bin" and eventually to really unlikely ones like "quo" and "pox".

In your case, probably do a frequency analysis on the dictionary of expected words, rather than all of English, with the slightly silly assumption that each word will occur exactly once if you don't have better information.
